title: If you have two instances of a service and both crash, how do you make the service fault tolerant (multi-node, Kubernetes self-healing, auto-scaling, health checks, multi-zone)?
shortTitle: If two instances of a service both crash, how do you make the service fault tolerant

s1_definition.profdef: Fault tolerance means the service keeps serving requests even when individual instances fail. The core techniques are running enough redundant instances spread across independent failure domains (multiple nodes and multiple availability zones), letting the orchestrator automatically detect dead instances through health probes and restart or reschedule them (Kubernetes self-healing), and automatically growing the number of instances under load (auto-scaling), so that the loss of even two instances is absorbed by survivors while the platform restores the lost capacity.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India runs a critical back-office processing room with two clerks. One morning both clerks fall sick at the same time, and work grinds to a halt. A fault-tolerant bank never relies on just two clerks in one room. It keeps clerks in several rooms across several buildings (multiple nodes and zones), a supervisor who constantly checks whether each clerk is actually working and instantly calls in a replacement when one stops (health checks and self-healing), and a staffing policy that pulls in extra clerks automatically when the queue gets long (auto-scaling). Now if two clerks drop, the others absorb the work and fresh clerks arrive within minutes, so Rajesh at the counter never notices.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fault tolerance comes from redundancy across independent failure domains plus a platform that automatically detects, replaces, and scales instances so losing some never means losing the service.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Fault tolerance means the service keeps serving requests even when individual instances fail. The core techniques are running enough redundant instances spread across independent failure domains (multiple nodes and multiple availability zones), letting the orchestrator automatically detect dead instances through health probes and restart or reschedule them (Kubernetes self-healing), and automatically growing the number of instances under load (auto-scaling), so that the loss of even two instances is absorbed by survivors while the platform restores the lost capacity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India runs a critical back-office processing room with two clerks. One morning both clerks fall sick at the same time, and work grinds to a halt. A fault-tolerant bank never relies on just two clerks in one room. It keeps clerks in several rooms across several buildings (multiple nodes and zones), a supervisor who constantly checks whether each clerk is actually working and instantly calls in a replacement when one stops (health checks and self-healing), and a staffing policy that pulls in extra clerks automatically when the queue gets long (auto-scaling). Now if two clerks drop, the others absorb the work and fresh clerks arrive within minutes, so Rajesh at the counter never notices.

**One line to remember:** Fault tolerance comes from redundancy across independent failure domains plus a platform that automatically detects, replaces, and scales instances so losing some never means losing the service.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is redundancy, and crucially, redundancy across independent failure domains. Running two instances on the same node gives you almost nothing, because if that node's hardware or kernel dies, both die together. In Kubernetes you spread replicas across nodes and across availability zones using pod anti-affinity and topology spread constraints. For example, a `topologySpreadConstraints` rule with `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone` forces the scheduler to place replicas in different zones so a whole-zone outage still leaves healthy pods.

Kubernetes self-healing is the automatic recovery loop. You declare a desired state, say three replicas, in a Deployment, and the controller continuously works to make reality match that declaration. If two pods crash, the ReplicaSet notices the actual count dropped to one and immediately creates two new pods to return to three. This is declarative recovery: you never manually restart anything. For example, `spec.replicas: 3` in a Deployment means Kubernetes will always drive the running count back to three.

Health checks are how the platform knows what "alive" and "ready" mean. A liveness probe answers "is this process healthy, or should it be killed and restarted?" A readiness probe answers "can this pod accept traffic right now?" A pod that is alive but still warming its connection pool reports not-ready so the Service stops routing to it until it is prepared. For example, a liveness probe hitting `/actuator/health/liveness` that fails three times triggers a restart, while a readiness probe on `/actuator/health/readiness` controls whether the pod is in the load-balancer rotation.

Auto-scaling restores and grows capacity. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler watches a metric like CPU or requests per second and changes the replica count to match demand. If a surge or a crash leaves the survivors overloaded, the HPA adds pods. Combined with the Cluster Autoscaler, which adds whole nodes when there is no room to schedule new pods, the system can recover from losing instances and from running out of machines.

Multi-node and multi-zone deployment is what makes the redundancy real. A node is one machine; a zone is a physically separate datacenter within a region with independent power and network. Spreading replicas across at least three nodes in at least three zones means a single machine failure or even a whole datacenter failure leaves healthy capacity. For the truly critical path you go multi-region, running the service in two regions behind a global load balancer so even a regional outage fails over.

Two more pieces complete the picture. A PodDisruptionBudget tells Kubernetes the minimum number of pods that must stay available during voluntary disruptions like node upgrades, so maintenance never accidentally takes you to zero. And the data layer must be fault tolerant too: a stateless service is easy to replicate, but the database behind it needs its own replication and failover, otherwise you have made the application resilient while leaving a single point of failure in storage.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the transfer service ran as exactly two instances on two pods. One night both pods happened to be scheduled on the same node, and that node's disk failed.

Problem 1 — both instances died at the same moment because they shared one failure domain, and transfers stopped entirely. This is exactly what multi-node and multi-zone spreading prevents: if replicas are forced onto different nodes and zones, a single node or zone failure can never take out all of them at once.

Problem 2 — even after the node recovered, nobody restarted the service, so the outage lasted until a human noticed. This is exactly what Kubernetes self-healing fixes: the Deployment's desired replica count means the controller recreates lost pods automatically within seconds, with no human in the loop.

Problem 3 — when a replacement pod started, it was added to the load balancer before its connection pool was warm, so the first requests failed. This is exactly what readiness probes fix: the pod stays out of rotation until it reports ready.

The mini-project simulates a `ServiceCluster` managing instances with a desired replica count, health probes, and zone placement. It builds an `InstanceSupervisor` that mimics the Kubernetes self-healing loop: it detects crashed instances and spawns replacements up to the desired count, respecting zone spread. The demo starts three instances across three zones, crashes two of them, and shows the supervisor restoring the count while a readiness gate keeps new instances out of rotation until warm.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the simulation
java -cp target/classes com.bank.faulttolerance.FaultToleranceDemo

# Apply the real Kubernetes manifests
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml

# Watch self-healing in action: delete two pods and see them recreated
kubectl get pods -l app=transfer-service -o wide
kubectl delete pod txn-abc txn-def
kubectl get pods -l app=transfer-service -o wide   # count returns to 3

# Check zone spread
kubectl get pods -l app=transfer-service \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,ZONE:.metadata.labels.zone
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a desired replica count of three, three zones (zone-a, zone-b, zone-c), and a simulated node failure that crashes two instances.

Step 1: The supervisor reconciles against an empty cluster. Live count is zero, desired is three, so it creates three instances, one in each zone for spread. They start in STARTING state.

Step 2: The instances finish warming and are marked READY. Readiness is what puts them in rotation, so the routable count is now three.

Step 3: A node fails, crashing two instances. Their status becomes CRASHED. The one survivor is still READY, so even in this moment the routable count is one and transfers still succeed, just with less headroom.

Step 4: The supervisor reconciles again. It sees live count is one but desired is three, so it creates two replacements, placing them in the zones that now have the fewest instances to preserve spread.

Step 5: The two new instances start in STARTING state, not READY. The readiness gate means the routable count is still one at this instant, so no traffic is sent to the cold instances and no requests fail on an unwarmed pool.

Step 6: The new instances finish warming and flip to READY. The routable count returns to three, fully restoring capacity, with the fleet spread across all three zones again.

```

       │                              │

       ▼                              ▼
   (not routable)                 [CRASHED] ──reconcile──→ new [STARTING]

  1. supervisor.reconcile()                 → 3 STARTING across zones
  2. markReady all                          → routable=3
  3. inst1.crash(); inst2.crash()           → live=1, routable=1
  4. supervisor.reconcile()
  5.   → cluster.liveInstances().size()==1  (< desired 3)
  6.   → addInstance() ×2 (least-loaded zones)
  7.   → new instances STARTING (routable still 1)
  8. markReady → routable=3 (restored, zone-spread)

    Pre:  cluster has a desired replica count
    Post: live instance count == desired (creates the shortfall)
    Invariant: new instances only routable after READY
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
If two instances both crash, the real lesson is that two instances were never enough, and the fix is fault tolerance built from redundancy across independent failure domains plus a platform that automatically detects, replaces, and scales. The first thing I check is whether the replicas are actually spread out. Running two pods on the same node gives almost no protection, because one node failure kills both. In Kubernetes I use pod anti-affinity and topology spread constraints so replicas land on different nodes and different availability zones, which means a single machine or even a whole datacenter failure still leaves healthy capacity serving traffic.

The second pillar is Kubernetes self-healing, which is a declarative reconciliation loop. I declare a desired replica count in the Deployment, say three, and the controller continuously drives the actual running count back to that number. When two pods crash, the ReplicaSet notices the count dropped to one and immediately creates two replacements, with no human involved. This is why I always frame fault tolerance as desired state rather than manual recovery.

Health probes make this precise. A liveness probe decides whether a pod should be killed and restarted, and a readiness probe decides whether a pod is allowed to receive traffic. The subtle but important point is that a freshly created replacement starts not-ready and stays out of the load-balancer rotation until its connection pool and caches are warm, so we never route requests to a cold instance and fail them. In our transfer service that readiness gate eliminated a whole class of first-request failures after scaling events.

Then auto-scaling restores and grows capacity. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler watches CPU or request rate and adds pods when survivors are overloaded, and the Cluster Autoscaler adds whole nodes when there is no room to schedule those pods. I also set a PodDisruptionBudget so that voluntary disruptions like node upgrades can never take me below a safe minimum, and I make sure the database behind the service has its own replication and failover, because resilient application instances in front of a single-point-of-failure database is a false sense of security.

The way I summarize it is this: run at least three replicas spread across at least three zones, let Kubernetes self-heal back to the desired count automatically, gate traffic with readiness probes, auto-scale to absorb surges and crashes, protect maintenance with a disruption budget, and make the data layer highly available too. With all of that, losing two instances becomes a brief dip in headroom that the survivors absorb while the platform restores full capacity within minutes, and the customer at the counter never notices.
